analytic.title: Extending response-time analysis for the automatic synthesis of functional graphs into fixed-priority distributed systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In this paper, we extend traditional response time analysis to a functional data flow graph (functional graph for brevity) mapped into a set of tasks. Different tasks synchronization semantics can be considered, depending on the way tasks synchronize on inputs consumed and outputs produced by functions in the functional graph. We study three different synchronization semantics and we give the appropriate response time analysis for functional graphs mapped into a set of preemptible fixed-priority tasks distributed over a priority-based network. Our response time analysis extension is needed to integrate response time constraints in an automatic approach for tasks synthesis. In this paper, for each semantics, the corresponding analysis is integrated in a tasks synthesis approach based on mathematical programming. Each semantics is evaluated against the minimum response time that can be obtained running task synthesis over a set of synthetic functional graphs. Finally, different sematics are considered and evaluated for an automotive case study.
Keywords-real-time distributed applications, response-time analysis, model-based development, automatic synthesis.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Model-based software design is an attractive solution to counteract the increasing complexity of distributed real-time systems development, especially when used in conjunction with a synthesis tool that automates the transition from a high-level functional model (representing the system functions and the signals exchanged among them), to a lowlevel operational model consisting of tasks and messages scheduled respectively onto execution nodes and buses [1]. A synthesis process as defined in industrial standards (like the automotive AUTOSAR [2]) and in academic frameworks (including the Platform-Based Design [3]) consists of three phases: i) the placement of functions on execution nodes and, respectively, of signals on buses; ii) the partitioning of functions into tasks and, respectively, of signals into messages; and finally, iii) the scheduling of tasks and messages. Note that each choice made during the three phases of the synthesis process has an impact on system schedulability, i.e. the capability to meet end-to-end deadlines. We consider a synthesis solution as valid (from a real-time point of view) if and only if all end-to-end deadlines, specified on end-to-end activation chains of functions, are met. Each chain is supposed to be activated by an external event (e.g. as detected by a sensor) or a timer, and terminating with the execution of a sink function. Verification of synthesis correctness relies on worst-case response time analysis, allowing to compute worst-case response times of each chain against end-to-end deadlines.

The functional model, constituting the entry point for the synthesis process, is often hidden for real-time scheduling researchers that indeed conceived response time analyses applied to a task model. Unfortunately, these traditional response time analyses (e.g., [4,5]) can be directly integrated in the synthesis process only when the entry point is restricted to a task model employed in real-time scheduling theory, i.e. when considering a one-to-one mapping of functions to tasks ( [6,7]. However, since the number of functions is usually huge, exploring how to cluster more functions in one task during synthesis is fundamental, and an appropriate analysis to verify synthesis validity is needed. For this purpose, we extend the fixed-priority analysis given in [4] to apply response time analysis to a functional graph mapped on a tasks graph, where more functions can be partitioned in a single task. Our proposal identifies different synchronization semantics for tasks depending on the way tasks synchronize on inputs consumed and outputs produced by functions in the functional graph. For each synchronization semantics a proper response analysis is derived. These analyses take into account the context switch effect, in order to properly analyze clustering benefits. Assuming a given synchronization semantics, we run a synthesis process based on mathematical programming that finds a synthesis solution minimizing response-time. Different semantics are then evaluated and compared in their ability of minimizing response times for some classes of graphs.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II gives related work. Section III introduces basic definitions and assumptions on the system model. Section IV presents the different task synchronization semantics and develops related response-time computation. Section V provides evaluation and comparison of different proposed semantics Section VI concludes the paper and discusses the future work.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Fixed-priority response time analysis has been widely discussed in the literature for mono-processor as well as for distributed architectures. Initially, Liu and al. [8] have proposed an analysis for independent periodic tasks running on a mono-processor. Later, many authors provided analysis for more complex task models. [9,10] and [11] address tasks with offsets (transactions). Tindell [9] suggested the model of tasks with static offsets. Palencia and Harbour [10] extended Tindell's work to consider tasks with dynamic offsets. Then, Turja and Nolin [11] proposed an improvement that reduces the pessimism of the upper bound defined by Tindell. In [12], authors proposed to use the real-time calculus for fixed priority scheduling in a monoprocessor architecture. In these analyses, transactions are linear in the sense that each task has at most one successor and one predecessor task. In [13,14], the SymTA/S analysis was proposed to handle non linear transactions. The analysis is able to deal with applications distributed across different types of networks (e.g., CAN, FlexRay, TTP) consisting of nodes that may use different scheduling policies (e.g., static cyclic scheduling, fixed priority preemptive scheduling, earliest deadline first). [15] gives a survey that covers hard real-time schedulability analysis techniques for multiprocessor systems. However, none of the above-cited analyses take into account the functional graph. Saksena et al. [16] faces the problem of extending response time analysis at functional level, nevertheless, it considers an object-oriented design model where the application is composed of a set of active objects communicating through asynchronous and synchronous message passing. This model requires an additional effort to extract end-to-end chains and to consider synchronous communications. Also, the analysis is quite complex to be integrated to a design process as it consider functions with not only priorities, but also with preemption thresholds to reduce the important blocking time due to the run-to-completion semantics considered for both objects and tasks. Besides, today's applications are increasingly expressed by a transaction model. Moreover, Saksena's analysis targets mono-processor systems.

On the other hand, several works on the scheduling of data flow graphs have been published. Parks and Lee [17] have studied the applicability of a non-preemptive Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling to data flow applications modeled as Synchronous Data Flow (SDF) graphs. The elements of the application graph are structured into independent periodic tasks. In [18] Goddard used Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling to analyze data flow programs modeled as PGM (Processing Graph Model) graphs mapped into a RBE (Rate-Based Execution) tasks model. The particularity of this task model is that each task is characterized by a rate of the form of x executions in y time units. Thus, scheduling analysis is done according to a processor demand. Later, Bamakhama et al. [19] have extended Goddard's approach to CSDF (Cyclo-Static Data Flow) graphs which are more expressive than PGM graphs, but they consider a strictly periodic task model. Bekooij et al. [20] have analyzed the impact of TDM scheduling on SDF graphs. They target soft real-time systems for which the data flow analysis is based on simulation. Moreira et al. [21] have addressed realtime scheduling of data flow applications modeled as SRDF (Single-Rate Data Flow) graphs. They have shown how the combination of static-order scheduling and TDM (Time Division Multiplexing) scheduling results in a scheduling strategy that improves the worst-case end-to-end response times compared to TDM scheduler in isolation. In [22], authors have considered priority-driven preemptive scheduling theory of periodic tasks to schedule data flow graphs. First, they proposed to compute an abstract affine schedule of the data flow graph by determining an affine relation between each pair of linked nodes in the graph, then this schedule is implemented by assigning period and phase to each function so that the graph becomes schedulable on a mono-processor system with an EDF or RM scheduler. However, the authors did not give any response-time computation, schedulability condition has been checked with respect to processor utilization factor that is sufficient for mono-processor systems. Actually, existing data flow graph analyses aims at finding the graph parameters (such as periods, start and end function's execution times, buffer size of channels) that allow the data flow graph to fit into the target task model which is often restricted to strictly periodic tasks (e.g. [18,19,22]). In our work, we preserve the data-driven execution semantics when synthesizing the tasks model without the need to redetermine the functions parameters, since we use a data-flow graph at task level as well. Moreover, in our work some current state-of-the-art limitations are overstepped such as: mono-processor execution platform ( [22]), deadlines less or equal than periods ( [22,19]), independent tasks model ( [17]), non preemptible tasks ( [17]), one-to-one mapping between functions and tasks ( [18,22]) and static-periodic scheduling ( [21,20]).

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: The considered system consists of two graphs, G and G , depicting respectively the network topology and the graph of functions activations.

The network topology is represented by an undirected graph G = (V, E), where V represents the set of execution nodes C ={c 1 , c 2 , ..., c c } and E is the set of communication buses by which execution nodes are connected β ={β 1 , β 2 ,..., β β }. Each execution node offers a set of real-time tasks 1 that perform the computation required by the system functions. Each task is characterized by a set of functions that it executes and τ i denotes the i th task in the system. The function τ (fi) returns the task to which the function f i belongs. In turn, communication buses offer a set of messages that realize the transmission of signals between remote tasks. Each message is defined by the set of signals that it transmits and µ i represents the i th message in the system. The function µ (si) returns the message transmitting the signal s i . When multiple tasks/messages share the same resource (node/bus), then two or more tasks/messages may request the resource at the same time. In order to arbitrate request conflicts, a resource is associated with a scheduler which selects a task/message to which it grants the resource out of the set of active tasks/messages according to some scheduling policy. Other active tasks/messages have to wait. In our model, each node runs a real-time operating system with a preemptive fixed-priority scheduling. Communication buses are assumed to be Controller Area Networks (CAN), arbitrated by priority. Therefore, tasks and messages are characterized by an execution priority level. The execution nodes and communication buses may have different processing and transmission speeds.

The functional graph (see Fig. 1) depicts the operational process of the system, in which events generated by sensors or by users trigger the computation of a set of control functions or algorithms, which eventually define a system response. This behavior may be captured by a synchronous data flow model, and described as a directed forest graph G = (V , E ), where V is the union of the functions F={f 1 ,f 2 ,...,f f } and the signals set Φ ={s 1 ,s 2 ,...,s s }. Functions (squares in Fig. 1) represent the atomic operations and signals (circles in Fig. 1) are their interactions. E denotes connections between functions and signals. snd(s i ) and rec(s i ) return, respectively, the sender function of signal s i and the list of its receiver functions, this latter contains at least one function. Each tree graph, so-called transaction, in G has a source node and a list of sink nodes, that conventionally represent the first and last functions. S={S 1 ,S 2 ,...,S S } ⊂ F denotes the set of system source functions. Functions and signals within a transaction are structured in one or more paths that represent the end-to-end executions of the system. A directed path ρ Si,fj from the source function S i to the sink function f j is a sequence of functions and signals ρ Si,fj = [S i , s i , f i+1 , s i+1 , f i+2 , ..., s j-1 , f j ] such that S i = snd(s i ) and f i+1 belongs to rec(s i ). Similarly, f i+1 = snd(s i+1 ) and f i+2 belongs to rec(s i+1 ) and so on till the underlying sink function f j belonging to rec(s j-1 ). γ = {ρ 1 , ρ 2 , ..., ρ ρ } denotes the set of system paths. Note that functions and signals of one transaction may belong to more than one path and multiple paths may exist between a couple of functions. A transaction may be linear (with only one path) or non-linear (with more than one path). In Fig. 1 the first transaction with ρ f1,f3 and the second one with ρ f4,f8 , ρ f4,f9 and ρ f4,f9 (here there are two different paths between f 4 and f 9 ) represent respectively a linear and non-linear transaction. A source function S i of each transaction is triggered by an external event e i that can be periodic or sporadic with, respectively, an activation period or a minimum inter-arrival time, denoted in both cases as P ei . The source function period is inherited by each function f i and signal s i belonging to the transaction, denoted respectively as P fi and P si i.e. functions and signals belonging to the same transaction have the same period. Furthermore, a deadline D i , that represents the end-to-end timing constraint on the execution of a path, is assigned to each path ρ i . This may be larger than the activation period ω fi = (ω fi,c1 , ω fi,c2 , ..., ω fi,cc ) and worstcase transmission times -→ ω si = (ω si,β1 , ω si,β2 , ..., ω si,β β ), where ω fi,cc and ω si,β β are respectively the worst-case execution time (WCET) of f i on node c c and the worst-case transmission time (WCTT) of s i on bus β β . Each function f i is executed with statically-assigned priority π fi inherited from its task. Therefore, functions within a task have the same priority. Similarly, signals within a message inherits its priority, π si is the priority of the signal s i . Signals are transmitted locally (dashed circles in Fig. 1) on an execution node, if the sender and all receiver functions are allocated to the same execution node, otherwise, they are transmitted remotely (complete circles in Fig. 1) on a communication bus. Note that a local signal may be transmitted either intertasks (all receiver functions are on tasks which are different from the task of the sender function) or intra-task (the sender and all receiver functions are executed by the same task). In this work, we consider a negligible cost for local communications. In Fig. 1, task/message for functions/remote signals are depicted to the left, and the allocation of functions/signals on execution nodes/buses is represented by different layouts. Functions/signals with the same layout are belonging to the same execution node/bus. The datadriven activation model [4] is considered for functions and signals. In this model, the source function of each transaction is triggered by an external event and subsequent functions are activated upon the reception of its incoming signals.

The reception of a signal corresponds to the completion of predecessor functions (if local signal) or the arrival of the message delivering the data for this signal (if remote signal). The sending of a message is triggered when all sender functions of signals transmitted by this message have completed their execution. Functions belonging to multiple paths may have an AND activation semantics i.e. they must wait for all incoming signals to be activated, or an OR activation semantics i.e. they are activated at the arrival of any incoming signal. A signal belonging to multiple paths is a signal with multiple receivers.

div.head: IV. RESPONSE-TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: The response-time analysis concerns the computation of functions and signals worst-case response times (WCRT) and then the deduction of worst-case end-to-end response times. To analyze our system, we extend the response time analysis with jitter propagation presented in [4]. In this paper, the analysis given in [4] has been adapted to consider the functional level, as applied to tasks and ignores the functional entities.

Please note that before computing functions WCRT, we apply the transformation given in [23] for functions with OR activation semantics. This transformation consists in separating the response sequences associated with each of the different incoming signals. All the sequence of functions and signals starting at the function with OR activation semantics are replicated and the number of replication is equal to the number of incoming signals. However, the transformation results in a functional graph without functions having OR activation semantics. Figure 2 shows an example of such transformation. The replicated functions and signals are added, respectively, to F and Φ. We define R fi /R si , the global WCRT of a function f i /signal s i , as the time taken from the activation of the external event until the execution of f i /s i completes in the worst case. The global WCRT of a function is computed as the maximum response time of all instances activated in the busy period [4]. This is due to the uncertainty about the instance which causes the WCRT. The response time of an instance q of a function f i (R q fi ) is defined based on the jitter term J fi , representing the delay between the arrival instant of the external event and the start instant of f q i , and the completion time W q fi which is the delay between the start and finish times of f q i (see equation ( 1)).

This caution consists in either enforcing the function and its replica to be implemented by the same task and thus ensuring their sequential execution, or adding a blocking time, corresponding to the execution time of the function, to the W term of both the function and its replica. This blocking time prevents the preemption of a function by its replica and vice versa.

div.head: D. Signals response-time analysis
div.p: Because of the non-preemptive scheduler within buses, the synchronization semantics of messages is of type Input N-of-N / output N-of-N. From the perspective of the response-time analysis, this implies that all signals transmitted by the same message have the same start transmission instant and the same end transmission instant. If a signal s i is transmitted remotely then its jitter is equal to the maximum WCRT of sender functions of signals transmitted by the same message as s i . The jitter of a local signal is equal to the WCRT of the sender function when it is transmitted inter-tasks and to the jitter of the sender function if it represents an intra-task communication.

div.head: E. Response-time analysis improvement
div.p: The WCRT computation presented above is quite pessimistic for the case of D ≤ P and this is due to the fact that a function f i undergoes twice the interferences from higher priority functions f k that precede in the same path (dp k,i = 1), once in the jitter and the other in the completion time computation. Actually, if D ≤ P then only one instance is considered during the W computation for functions and signals (i.e. q * = 1). Moreover, higher priority functions that precede f i in the same path can be reactivated only after the completion of f i , so they cannot preempt f i . To consider this improvement, the main thing to do is to remove functions f l that are on the same path as f i ( (i) ∩ (l) = ∅) from the set hp(f i ) in equations ( 7), ( 6) and ( 4). In addition, for the third semantics, the value of

div.p: in the third term of equation ( 4) becomes equal to 1. The same improvement may be considered for signals.

Generally response time analyses ignore the execution time required by the scheduler and assume an instant context switch. In our case, the context switch cost has an impact on the synthesis solution. For this purpose, the function response-time analysis, presented above, may be refined to consider the context switch overhead in the completion time computation. According to [24,25], three blocks need to be considered. Firstly, the scheduler execution time to choose which function will be schedule. Second, the time it takes to perform the context switch of the chosen function. Finally, the time it takes to perform the context switch away from the executing function. In [26], the effect of the context switch is included in the analysis by simply incrementing the execution times by an amount equal to 2CS, where CS is the worst-case context switching time. Based on [24,25] and [26], we add 2CS to the first and last terms in W fi formulas i.e ω fi,cj in the first term of equations ( 7), ( 6) and ( 4) becomes ω fi,cj + 2CS and ω f k ,cj in their last term becomes ω f k ,cj + 2CS.

div.head: V. EVALUATION
div.p: This section starts with a qualitative comparison of the three synchronization semantics, then experimental results of the synthesis of these semantics is presented. Finally, an automotive case study is used to illustrate each semantics.

div.head: A. Qualitative semantics comparison
div.p: The differences between these three tasks synchronization semantics in terms of WCRTs results are mentioned with respect to a fixed synthesis solution. First, in the Fig. 8, we give for each semantics the pseudo code of the task τ 2 of the example presented in Fig. 7. For the first semantics, the task may have two different jitters that correspond respectively to the arrival of s 1 and s 2 (WaitForAny), while for the second and the third ones, the task jitter depends on the arrival instant of both s 1 and s 2 (WaitForAll). Furthermore, in the first semantics, as it is unknown which signal among s 1 and s 2 arrives first, the worst-case leads to the consideration of a bilateral waiting between f 3 and f 4 , the waiting may be multiple because s 1 may arrive multiple times before the arrival of s 2 and vice versa. In the second one, s 3 may be delivered before or after the processing of s 2 depending on the execution order of f 3 and f 4 i.e. unilateral waiting. Finally, in the third semantics, the results of s 1 and s 2 processing are delivered at the same time at the end of τ 2 execution, thus there is a bilateral waiting between f 3 and f 4 . In a more general way, we can Input N-of-N/output N-of-N (N N/N N ) vs. input N-of-N/output 1-of-N (N N/1N ): the synchronization point at the entry of τ 2 for both N N/N N and N N/1N avoids multiple interferences between parallel functions within the task. So, as N N/N N leads to a bilateral waiting in this case, we can say that N N/1N gives always better WCRTs than N N/N N when a task contains functions belonging to different paths.

Input N-of-N/output N-of-N (N N/N N ) vs. input 1-of-N/output 1-of-N (1N/1N ): when the delay related to the synchronization point to the entry of τ 2 in N N/N N is more important than the delay caused by the multiple interferences between parallel functions within the task in 1N/1N , then 1N/1N gives better WCRTs results than N N/N N . Otherwise, N N/N N is more efficient than 1N/1N .

Input N-of-N/output 1-of-N (N N/1N ) vs. input 1-of-N/output 1-of-N (1N/1N ): if the difference between the arrival instants of input signals to τ 2 in N N/1N is negligible, then we can conclude that N N/1N is more efficient than 1N/1N . Otherwise, it is necessary to measure the tradeoff between the delay caused by the synchronization point at the entry of the task in N N/1N and the delay due to the multiple bilateral waiting in 1N/1N .
In this subsection, we have presented a comparison with respect to a precise significant case, other cases are discussed in the following section.

div.head: B. Synthesis experimental results
div.p: The objective of this experiment is to assess the impact of each task's synchronization semantics, and consequently the appropriate response time analysis, on a synthesis solution. For this purpose, we first integrated our analysis to the synthesis approach presented in [1]. This is an Mixed Integer Linear Programming based approach that returns an optimal solution for: i) the placement of functions and signals respectively on the executions nodes and buses, ii) the partitioning of function into tasks and signals into messages, and finally, iii) the priority assignment to tasks and messages, and this with respect to the minimal average of response times. Then, we randomly generated applications of 5, 10 and 15 functions on execution platforms with 2, 4, 6 and 8 execution nodes linked according to bus, ring or fully connected network topology. A total of 10 applications were generated for each dimension, thus, a total of 360 applications were used for evaluating the impact of each semantics. The structure of the functional model, expressed by the number of transactions and the number of functions and signals on each transaction, and the functional parameters such as periods, WCETs and WCTTs, were generated according to the uniform law. We were interested in comparing the quality of the obtained synthesis solutions under consideration of the different semantics. This quality is measured by the value of the average of response times representing the optimization metric. After analyzing the solutions of the 360 instances, we found that these can be classified into four main cases. The values mentioned above squares and circles are respectively the WCETs and WCTTs.
1) Case 1: Identical synthesis result is obtained for all semantics in the following circumstances:

• Independent functions with non-harmonic periods. The solution consists in putting each function on a different task. Because of harmonic rates constraints, there are no other alternatives, thus, there are no differences between the three semantics. 2) Case 2: N N/N N and 1N/1N return the same result and N N/1N returns a result with better performance:

• Independent functions with harmonic periods. Through the functions execution order defined within tasks, N N/1N favors the partitioning of independent functions with harmonic periods into the same task as this leads to less context switch effect and to no bilateral waiting between functions of a task. On the contrary, the others semantics prevent this kind of partitioning because of the presence of a bilateral waiting. Therefore, N N/1N returns solutions for which the context switch effect is reduced in comparison with the solutions referred by N N/N N and 1N/1N . • A single signal is sent to different receiver functions.

When the communication on the network results in a less efficient solutions, the nature of a signal that requires it to be transmitted either intra-task or intertasks leads to only two possible solutions: putting all functions (sender and receivers) of the signal on the same task or putting each function on different task. N N/N N and 1N/1N opt for the second solution as the first one leads to a bilateral waiting between functions of the task and so to a worse solution, while N N/1N chooses the first solution that results in a reduced context switches cost compared to that of the solution returned by N N/N N and 1N/1N . 3) Case 3: N N/1N returns the most efficient result, 1N/1N sends the least efficient one and N N/N N provides a result of an intermediate performance:

div.head: C. Response-time analysis of Cruise Control System
div.p: To illustrate our proposal we consider an automotive distributed hard real-time system which is the cruise control system (CCS) given in [27]. This section shows the impact of each semantics on the quality of a given synthesis solution, then it highlights the difference between the three semantics.

Description: the CCS automatically stabilizes the vehicle speed according to the driver's desired set speed. Functional model of CCS is composed of two linear transactions, the first one contains six functions (Input acquisition, Input interpretation, Speed setpoint, Application condition, Basic function and Controller) and five signals, the second is formed by two functions (Diagnosis and Limp home) and one signal. The hardware architecture of the platform model is composed of two Electronic control units (ECU), which represent execution nodes, (Body controller ECU and Engine management ECU) linked by one CAN bus. The mapping of the functional graph on the network topology is depicted on the figure 9. Table I presents the system real-time parameters. WCTT for signals is fixed to 4 ms. A message priority is equal to the sender task priority. Please note that we set the context switch cost to 0, 5. Discussion of results: the CCS response-time analysis results considering the different semantics are given in table II. Although output 1-of-N case (1N/1N and N N/1N ) leads to better WCRT for input acquisition function, it does not impact the WCRT of the acquisition task (i.e. Input interpretation function). Whatever semantics is considered, the WCRT of the acquisition task is the same. From the controller task point of view, we obtained better completion times for Application condition and Basic function intermediate functions with 1N/1N and N N/1N than with N N/N N . This is due to the bilateral waiting between functions on different paths belonging to the same task in the case of output N-of-N (N N/N N ). However, the Controller function completion time is the same for the three semantics which leads to the same latency of the first path (34, 27). In other words, a better WCRT for intermediate functions does not improve the latency value as the only result counts is the WCRT of the last function in the path. Finally, input 1of-N case (1N/1N ) has considerably improved the WCRT of Limp home function and thus the second path latency (19,95). This improvement is due to the jitter value since the function does not wait for the arrival of S 3 as is the case of input N-of-N. Moreover, even the completion time obtained under N N/1N is less than the one returned by 1N/1N (thanks to the execution order defined between task functions), the delay caused by the jitter is greater in the case of N N/1N compared to 1N/1N . At the end, we have considered the synthesis optimisation of the CCS. The obtained results showed that our synthesis solution considering the different semantics gives better latencies with respect to the original solution. Both 1N/1N and NN/NN semantics led to 30, 27 and 16, 55 as latency for the first and the second path, respectively. The NN/1N semantics returned solution with 28, 27 and 17, 37, respectively.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: We have presented an extension of a traditional response time analysis for distributed systems in order to address a functional data flow graph mapped into a set of data-driven tasks. This proposal is essential to consider schedulability constraints during the automatic synthesis of a lower level operational model in a model-based approach. According to the instants at which a task produces and consumes functional data, we have considered three different tasks synchronization semantics and for each semantics we gave the corresponding response time analysis. We have discussed the impact of a given semantics on the performance of a synthesis solution and we have shown that the benefit of considering one semantic instead of the others depends on the jitters and interferences values, which in turn depend on timing parameters like periods and WCETs. Finally, we have evaluated each semantic with respect to the obtained minimal average of response times in the context of an automatic synthesis approach based on mathematical programming.

To increase system performance with respect to minimum response time, we suggest for future work to develop an optimization technique to assign different synchronization semantics to system's tasks. This leads to applications with a mixture of synchronization semantics for tasks.

For N N/1N and 1N/1N semantics, even if the result of an intermediate function 2 may be available before the execution start of the subsequent functions, the only result that counts for the response time computation is the response time of the last activated function in the path. A function sends multiple signals, each one has its own receiver function which is different than the receiver of the others signals. Moreover, the communication cost is significant in relation to execution times. In the solution returned by N N/1N , all signals are transmitted intratask which decreases the cost of context switches without considering the effect of a bilateral waiting. N N/N N and 1N/1N are forced to return a solution with more tasks to avoid this effect of bilateral waiting. N N/N N and 1N/1N provide the same solution but of different qualities. This is because N N/N N results in smaller context switching than 1N/1N since the delay from the receiver functions partitioned with the sender function is included in the jitter. 1N/1N considers this delay in the interferences term which implies an increasing in the context switches cost. For example, with 1N/1N , f 3 and f 4 can preempt the execution of f 2 since f 2 and f 3 can be activated at the same time, while in N N/N N , f 2 cannot start executing before the execution end of f 3 and f 4 . This implies that the delay from f 4 and f 3 is included in the jitter of f 2 as f 3 and f 4 belong to the same task as f 1 . 1N/1N results in two additional context switches with respect to N N/N N .
